newsitem.title: INDIA: Peru's Fujimori says third term not a priority.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori says third term not a priority.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori said on Monday that working towards another term in office, currently not permitted under the constitution, was not a priority for him.
"Amending the constitution is not easy," Fujimori, who won a second term in presidential elections in 1995, told a news conference in the Indian capital.
"I am concentrating my attention on fighting poverty and unemployment," he said in response to a question on a third term. "It (another term in office) is not at the moment my first priority."

Elections are not due until 2000. Fujimori, who championed the formation of a new constitution in 1993, was first elected in 1990 and won his second term by defeating former United Nations secretary-general Javier Perez de Cuellar.
Fujimori, who arrived in New Delhi on Sunday for a four-day official visit, said he had no news on leftist guerrilla leader Hugo Avellaneda, who is wanted by police.

Avellaneda is the top leader of the left-wing Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA). The previous chief, Nestor Cerpa, was killed by Peruvian troops at the end of a 127-day standoff on April 22 to free 72 hostages held in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima.

"We are offering around $80,000 for the information so we may capture him. I don't know if he is captured already. I don't have this information because of the difference of hours between Peru and India," Fujimori said.
He also said there was no information on the leader of the Maoist Shining Path, Oscar Ramirez "Feliciano", who is said to be seriously ill with a tropical disease.
"Again in this, we are going to have a reward of $100,000," he said.
Peru made a major breakthrough in 1992 with the arrest of Abimael Guzman, then Shining Path leader, which brought under control 13 years of Maoist insurgency that shook Peru.
Fujimori slammed human rights organisations for criticising Peru's human rights record, linked to alleged excesses in its action to contain armed insurgency.
"We have to combat terrorism respecting human rights but we cannot put aside human rights of the society," he said.
"During 13 years, no human rights organisation said anything about the human rights of 24 million Peruvian people. No one. Neither America's (Human Rights) Watch nor Amnesty International," he said.

Fujimori said Peru was committed to a free trade zone covering North and South America by 2005, but was not in a hurry to re-join the Andean Pact regional free trade grouping, from which it broke away in 1992.
"We are for integration but in a very much open way," Fujimori said.
Peru failed to reach an agreement on re-joining last month at a meeting of the Andean Pact, which comprises Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador and Venezuela.
